title: Beautifying Transportation Infrastructure Council
summary:
The U.S. Department of Transportation is creating a new Beautifying Transportation Infrastructure Council to advise the Secretary on how to make highways, bridges, and transit hubs more attractive without sacrificing safety or efficiency. Nominations to serve on the council are open now and due by November 21, 2025. Separately, the Postal Regulatory Commission announced new USPS shipping contract filings and opened a short public comment period through October 24, 2025.

This council is meant to bring together architects, landscape designers, urban planners, artists, engineers, preservation voices, and representatives from state, local, and Tribal governments. It will meet twice a year, identify best practices, suggest design and funding priorities, and offer ways to measure design quality. Up to 11 members will serve two-year terms, with a goal of balanced viewpoints and no single group in charge. Meetings are expected to be virtual or hybrid, and the department may set up smaller working groups to tackle specific tasks. The nomination package is short—a brief bio, a letter of support, contact details, and a statement that the nominee meets the criteria—and more details are available on regulations.gov.

Who stands to benefit? Communities and travelers could see more welcoming public spaces that reflect local character, potentially improving quality of life, boosting civic pride, and supporting nearby businesses. Designers, artists, and engineers may gain a formal channel to influence projects, while state, local, and Tribal leaders can bring community needs into early planning.

Who might have concerns? Some will worry that a focus on appearance could add costs, slow delivery, or compete with maintenance and safety priorities. Smaller communities may fear a one‑size‑fits‑all approach or new design rules that are hard to meet. There may also be questions about how “beauty” is measured and who gets to decide.

On the postal side, the new USPS contract filings could eventually shape shipping options and pricing for businesses and consumers, but the details are limited and some materials are sealed. Supporters may see this as routine competition that can improve service, while others may raise transparency concerns or note the very short window for public comment.

Overall, the notice signals an effort to elevate design in public infrastructure, while routine postal regulatory actions continue on a tight timetable.
